# Angular close-up style guide

Use this distinct painting treatment when the user asks for an earth-toned
angular portrait, the saved close-up self-portrait style, or hyper-closeups
of people and objects made from interlocking clay and ivory planes.
Use this treatment independently of flowing figurative artwork.

## Visual reference and scope

Inspect [the saved generated close-up](../assets/styles/earth-toned-angular-portrait.png)
before preparing a prompt. The user selected this result to retain as another
painting style. It demonstrates a treatment, not a likeness template or a
requirement to repeat its exact polygon arrangement.

This reference was generated from a user-supplied painting. The original source
is not bundled with this skill. Do not infer artist identity, physical medium,
historical movement, or a license from its appearance.

## Construction

- For portraits, default to one face in an extreme close-up. Crop through forehead, cheek,
  and lower jaw so the head continues outside the image. Omit shoulders and
  setting unless requested.
- Build recognition from a few unequal, interlocking planes rather than a
  complete anatomical head. Mix broad quadrilaterals, blunt wedges, stepped
  edges, and occasional restrained curves; avoid a uniform triangle mesh.
- Let one edge serve adjacent features: brow becomes an eye recess boundary,
  the nose turns into a cheek edge, and the cheek redirects toward the chin.
  Invent these relationships instead of tracing the reference.
- Contrast one broad quiet pale cheek mass with smaller warm fragments and a
  few tapered near-black recesses. Do not outline every plane equally.
- Use a compressed dark eye aperture under an off-axis brow, a long bent or
  stepped nose construction, and a small displaced mouth interruption.
  A detailed iris, realistic nostrils, or modeled lips are not required.
- For a single portrait, preserve a coherent single-face reading despite mixed
  viewpoints. Do not accidentally introduce extra faces or interpret dark
  wedges as wounds.

## Angular hyper-closeups set

The user retained these five generated experiments as a separate learning set
within the earth-toned angular treatment. They extend its vocabulary beyond
single portraits to contact, playing an instrument, and everyday objects.
Inspect the example matching the requested subject; do not send all five to

| [Two faces touching](../assets/styles/angular-hyper-closeups/two-faces-touching.png) | A narrow dark contact boundary connects a compressed eye/nose fragment to a broad pale cheek. | The second face is highly ambiguous; preserve enough separate cues if two people must read immediately. |
| [Hand against a face](../assets/styles/angular-hyper-closeups/hand-against-face.png) | Long unequal finger planes oppose a quiet cheek; the small dark eye opening anchors recognition. | Do not copy its triangular pupil as a universal eye symbol or turn every finger into a beveled block. |
| [Guitarist's fingers](../assets/styles/angular-hyper-closeups/guitarist-fingers.png) | Fine parallel strings cut across larger hand planes; a cropped sound-hole arc reveals the instrument. | Keep contact and hand ownership readable. These blocky fingers are not anatomical or fingering references. |
| [An embrace](../assets/styles/angular-hyper-closeups/embrace.png) | A large pale shoulder and smaller angular hand make contact readable through overlap and a dark seam. | The second person is only suggested; do not claim a clearly readable pair of full figures. |
| [Worn sneaker](../assets/styles/angular-hyper-closeups/worn-sneaker.png) | A broad toe plane stays quiet while crossed laces and small dark recesses identify the near-abstract subject. | Preserve object-specific cues rather than importing eyes, noses, or other portrait fragments. |

These are unchanged generated outputs, not photographs or additional original
source paintings. Retaining them approves their use as learning examples, not
every surface detail. They show stronger texture and more block-like relief
than the base portrait in places; do not make uniform heavy texture or 3-D
bevels mandatory.

For a new subject, choose one broad quiet plane, a few smaller interruptions,
and one revealing cue. Crop until the image approaches abstraction while that
cue still supports recognition. Adapt planes to the subject rather than using
a face-shaped template. No added eyes on objects, explanatory background, or
full-object outline is needed unless requested.

## Color and surface

Use dusty terracotta, muted rose/clay, warm sienna, chalky ivory, and charcoal.
Give them unequal areas: broad pale planes, warm supporting fields, and small
deep-dark wedges. These are relationships, not measured color specifications.
Honor an explicitly requested alternate palette without changing the construction.

Keep the surface matte and tactile. Allow subtle pigment variation, rubbed or
scumbled coverage, dry-brush drag, and localized dark edge reinforcement.
Allow gentle tonal variation within a plane rather than relying on
scratchy outlines or uniformly flat fills. Keep plane boundaries
legible; do not turn them into smoothly shaded 3-D bevels or realistic skin volume.

Avoid uniform noise, artificial cracks, glossy reflections, dense hatching
everywhere, and an anatomical portrait hidden under a distressed filter.
The image should feel close, quiet, and introspective, not mechanically faceted.

## Delayed discovery and abstract rhythm

Use this treatment when a second person or relationship should emerge after the
dominant subject, not when the requested people must all read immediately.
Inspect the retained
[hidden embrace](../assets/final-paintings/hidden-embrace-echoed-hair.png)
for hierarchy and echoed shapes, not its repetitive surface pattern.

- Establish a reading order: dominant face, abstract rhythm, then a smaller
  relationship discovered through contact. Keep the primary eye/cheek contrast
  stronger than the secondary clues; balance visual weight, not equal areas.
- Suggest a hidden head through a few coordinated cues such as a cropped crown,
  small ear, narrowing nape, and shoulder overlap. An isolated mark is not
  enough, but a complete eye-nose-mouth profile can reveal the person too soon.
  Let occlusion hide structure rather than fading a finished portrait.
- Keep secondary hair close in hue and value to neighboring planes. Allow some
  boundaries to disappear while retaining enough crown-to-ear-to-nape continuity
  to support discovery. For requested long hair, use a broad descending taper,
  not a high-contrast cap or detailed strands. Hair and accessories can suggest
  the requested character's styling; they do not establish gender universally.
- Echo the hair's hue, broad bend, and unequal taper in smaller abstract planes
  elsewhere, away from the hidden head. A visual rhyme can camouflage the clue
  as part of the composition. Do not copy the full silhouette, add another head,
  mirror the layout mechanically, or draw a ribbon connecting the two areas.
- Place a competing color accent away from the concealed person. Bright foliage
  or a contrasting patch around their head can spotlight it instead of distract.
  Integrate arcs or broken passages into shared plane boundaries rather than
  laying a decorative stripe over the face. Keep accents subordinate to the
  main face and preserve broad quiet areas.
- Share palette colors across figures rather than assigning each person a
  separate hue. Warm-cool contrast can enrich the painting without outlining
  the hidden relationship. Change color emphasis without multiplying swatches
  or filling every plane with equal saturation.
- Check ambiguous tangencies: a tapered dark strip below an ear may read as
  facial hair, while a dangling accent may resemble an anatomical fragment.
  Simplify or merge that local edge into the neck; adding jewelry is not the
  only way to clarify a character. Keep the main face's necessary dark recesses.

For landscape adaptations, extend and rebalance peripheral planes instead of
stretching the face or rotating the whole painting. Preserve the revealing
features and intentional crop; introduce a shoulder only when the requested
contact or embrace needs it.

For revisions, name the affected region and preserve the accepted hierarchy.
Do not accumulate every earlier corrective instruction into the next prompt.
Repeated image edits can amplify crackle and embossed noise: distinguish a
composition reference from a surface reference, and explicitly retain quiet
matte fields rather than treating the newest texture as authoritative.

## Prompt starter

> Create one original extreme-close-up portrait using the attached angular
> painting as a construction and surface reference, not a tracing template.
> Fill the image with a single cropped face built from unequal interlocking
> clay, terracotta, ivory, and charcoal planes. Let a compressed eye recess,
> stepped nose edge, broad pale cheek, and faint mouth share boundaries and
> pass a diagonal movement through the composition. Use mixed viewpoints,
> matte rubbed pigment, selective dark wedges, and varied edge emphasis.
> Invent the arrangement. No complete oval head, realistic anatomy, uniform
> triangulation, glossy bevels, lettering, or decorative background.

Adapt subject and framing to the request. If a photograph is supplied, use its
topic and any explicitly required features without restoring photographic
anatomy or likeness by default. Supply this variant's reference to the image
tool rather than automatically adding unrelated art references.

## Inspection

Check that the requested subject and person count read, the crop is genuinely
close, the planes share meaningful boundaries, and a dominant quiet area contrasts with
smaller angular interruptions. Confirm texture supports rather than conceals
the construction. Do not claim exact likeness or fidelity without evidence.

For delayed-discovery scenes, check both first and second readings: does the
dominant subject lead, and can the secondary head/contact actually be found?
Check whether echoed shapes camouflage the clue or instead frame and spotlight
it. Describe ambiguity honestly; do not claim a surprising discovery is guaranteed.
Inspect the actual output before claiming a requested edit worked. If image
inspection is unavailable, state that limitation rather than inventing findings.

Generate only on an explicit image request; saving this style does not authorize
new paid trials. Deliver the actual image or working link and disclose misses.
